text: Such women never remain unmarried,—it is the law of their nature to marry,—their husband is their first lover, and he is always to blame for anything that may happen afterwards; the unfaithful wife herself being invariably absolutely in the right, and of course perfectly innocent.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: So thought Velchaninoff; and he was convinced that such a type of woman actually existed; but he was no less convinced that there also existed a corresponding type of men, born to be the husbands of such women.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: In his opinion the mission of such men was to be, so to speak, “permanent husbands,”—that is, to be husbands all their lives, and nothing else.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff had not the smallest doubt as to the existence of these two types, and Pavel Pavlovitch Trusotsky was, in his opinion, an excellent representative of the male type.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Of course, the Pavel Pavlovitch of last night was by no means the same Pavel Pavlovitch as he had known at T——.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He had found an extraordinary change in the man; and yet, on reflection, he was bound to admit that the change was but natural, for that he could only have remained what he was so long as his wife lived; and that now he was but a part of a whole, allowed to wander at will—that is, an imperfect being, a surprising, an incomprehensible sort of a thing, without proper balance.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: As for the Pavel Pavlovitch of T——, this is what Velchaninoff remembered of him:

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch had been a husband, of course,—a formality,—and that was all.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: If, for instance, he was a clerk of department besides, he was so merely in his capacity of, and as a part of his responsibility as—a husband.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He worked for his wife, and for her social position.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He had been thirty-five years old at that time, and was possessed of some considerable property.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He had not shown any special talent, nor, on the other hand, any marked incapacity in his professional employment; his position had been decidedly a good one.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Natalia Vasilievna had been respected and looked up to by all; not that she valued their respect in the least,—she considered it merely as her due.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: She was a good hostess, and had schooled Pavel Pavlovitch into polite manners, so that he was able to receive and entertain the very best society passably well.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He might be a clever man, for all Velchaninoff knew, but as Natalia Vasilievna did not like her husband to talk much, there was little opportunity of judging.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He may have had many good qualities, as well as bad; but the good ones were, so to speak, kept put away in their cases, and the bad ones were stifled and not allowed to appear.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff remembered, for instance, that Pavel Pavlovitch had once or twice shown a disposition to laugh at those about him, but this unworthy proclivity had been very promptly subdued.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He had been fond of telling stories, but this was not allowed either; or, if permitted at all, the anecdote was to be of the shortest and most uninteresting description.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch had a circle of private friends outside the house, with whom he was fain, at times, to taste the flowing bowl; but this vicious tendency was radically stamped out as soon as possible.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: And yet, with all this, Natalia Vasilievna appeared, to the uninitiated, to be the most obedient of wives, and doubtless considered herself so.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch may have been desperately in love with her,—no one could say as to this.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff had frequently asked himself during his life at T——, whether Pavel Pavlovitch ever suspected his wife of having formed the tie with himself, of which mention has been made.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff had several times questioned Natalia Vasilievna on this point, seriously enough; but had invariably been told, with some show of annoyance, that her husband neither did know, nor ever could know; and that “all there might be to know was not his business!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Another trait in her character was that she never laughed at Pavel Pavlovitch, and never found him funny in any sense; and that she would have been down on any person who dared to be rude to him, at once!

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch’s reference to the pleasant little readings enjoyed by the trio nine years ago was accurate; they used to read Dickens’ novels together.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff or Trusotsky reading aloud, while Natalia Vasilievna worked.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The life at T—— had ended suddenly, and so far as Velchaninoff was concerned, in a way which drove him almost to the verge of madness.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The fact is, he was simply turned out—although it was all managed in such a way that he never observed that he was being thrown over like an old worn-out shoe.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: A young artillery officer had appeared in the town a month or so before Velchaninoff’s departure and had made acquaintance with the Trusotsky’s.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The trio became a quartet.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Before long Velchaninoff was informed that for many reasons a separation was absolutely necessary; Natalia Vasilievna adduced a hundred excellent reasons why this had become unavoidable—and especially one which quite settled the matter.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: After his stormy attempt to persuade Natalia Vasilievna to fly with him to Paris—or anywhere,—Velchaninoff had ended by going to St. Petersburg alone—for two or three months at the very most, as he said,—otherwise he would refuse to go at all, in spite of every reason and argument Natalia might adduce.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Exactly two months later Velchaninoff had received a letter from Natalia Vasilievna, begging him to come no more to T——, because that she already loved another.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: As to the principal reason which she had brought forward in favour of his immediate departure, she now informed him that she had made a mistake.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff remembered the young artilleryman, and understood,—and so the matter had ended, once and for all.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: A year or two after this Bagantoff appeared at T——, and an intimacy between Natalia Vasilievna and the former had sprung up which lasted for five years.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: This long period of constancy, Velchaninoff attributed to advancing age on the part of Natalia.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He sat on the side of his bed for nearly an hour and thought.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: At last he roused himself, rang for Mavra and his coffee, drank it off quickly—dressed—and punctually at eleven was on his way to the Pokrofsky Hotel: he felt rather ashamed of his behaviour to Pavel Pavlovitch last night.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff put down all that phantasmagoria of the trying of the lock and so on to Pavel Pavlovitch’s drunken condition and to other reasons,—but he did not know why he was now on his way to make fresh relations with the husband of that woman, since their acquaintanceship and intercourse had come to so natural and simple a termination; yet something seemed to draw him thither—some strong current of impulse,—and he went.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch was not thinking of “running away,” and goodness knows why Velchaninoff should have asked him such a question last night—he did not know himself why he had said it!

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He was directed to the Petrofsky Hotel, and found the building at once.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: At the hotel he was told that Pavel Pavlovitch had now engaged a furnished lodging in the back part of the same house.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Mounting the dirty and narrow stairs indicated, as far as the third storey, he suddenly became aware of someone crying.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: It sounded like the weeping of a child of some seven or eight years of age; it was a bitter, but a more or less suppressed sort of crying, and with it came the sound of a grown man’s voice, apparently trying to quiet the child—anxious that its sobbing and crying should not be heard,—and yet only succeeding in making it cry the louder.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The man’s voice did not seem in any way sympathetic with the child’s grief; and the latter appeared to be begging for forgiveness.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Making his way into a narrow dark passage with two doors on each side of it, Velchaninoff met a stout-looking, elderly woman, in very careless morning attire, and inquired for Pavel Pavlovitch.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: She tapped the door with her fingers in response to his inquiry—the same door, apparently, whence issued the noises just mentioned.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Her fat face seemed to flush with indignation as she did so.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “He appears to be amusing himself in there!” she said, and proceeded downstairs.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff was about to knock, but thought better of it and opened the door without ceremony.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: In the very middle of a room furnished with plain, but abundant furniture, stood Pavel Pavlovitch in his shirt-sleeves, very red in the face, trying to persuade a little girl to do something or other, and using cries and gestures, and what looked to Velchaninoff very like kicks, in order to effect his purpose.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The child appeared to be some seven or eight years of age, and was poorly dressed in a short black stuff frock.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: She seemed to be in a most hysterical condition, crying and stretching out her arms to Pavel Pavlovitch, as though begging and entreating him to allow her to do whatever it might be she desired.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: On Velchaninoff’s appearance the scene changed in an instant.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: No sooner did her eyes fall on the visitor than the child made for the door of the next room, with a cry of alarm; while Pavel Pavlovitch—thrown out for one little instant—immediately relaxed into smiles of great sweetness—exactly as he had done last night, when Velchaninoff suddenly opened his front door and caught him standing outside.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Alexey Ivanovitch!” he cried in real surprise; “who ever would have thought it! Sit down—sit down—take the sofa—or this chair,—sit down, my dear sir! I’ll just put on——” and he rushed for his coat and threw it on, leaving his waistcoat behind.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Don’t stand on ceremony with me,” said Velchaninoff sitting down; “stay as you are!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “No, sir, no! excuse me—I insist upon standing on ceremony. There, now! I’m a little more respectable! Dear me, now, who ever would have thought of seeing you here!—not I, for one!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch sat down on the edge of a chair, which he turned so as to face Velchaninoff.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “And pray why shouldn’t you have expected me? I told you last night that I was coming this morning!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I thought you wouldn’t come, sir—I did indeed; in fact, when I thought over yesterday’s visit, I despaired of ever seeing you again: I did indeed, sir!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff glanced round the room meanwhile.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The place was very untidy; the bed was unmade; the clothes thrown about the floor; on the table were two coffee tumblers with the dregs of coffee still in them, and a bottle of champagne half finished, and with a tumbler standing alongside it.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He glanced at the next room, but all was quiet there; the little girl had hidden herself, and was as still as a mouse.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “You don’t mean to say you drink that stuff at this time of day?” he asked, indicating the champagne bottle.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “It’s only a remnant,” explained Pavel Pavlovitch, a little confused.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “My word! You are a changed man!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Bad habits, sir; and all of a sudden. All dating from that time, sir. Give you my word, I couldn’t resist it. But I’m all right now—I’m not drunk—I shan’t talk twaddle as I did last night; don’t be afraid sir, it’s all right! From that very day, sir; give you my word it is! And if anyone had told me half a year ago that I should become like this,—if they had shown me my face in a glass then as I should be now, I should have given them the lie, sir; I should indeed!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Hem! Then you were drunk last night?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Yes—I was!” admitted Pavel Pavlovitch, a little guiltily—“not exactly drunk, a little beyond drunk!—I tell you this by way of explanation, because I’m always worse after being drunk! If I’m only a little drunk, still the violence and unreasonableness of intoxication come out afterwards, and stay out too; and then I feel my grief the more keenly. I daresay my grief is responsible for my drinking. I am capable of making an awful fool of myself and offending people when I’m drunk. I daresay I seemed strange enough to you last night?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Don’t you remember what you said and did?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Assuredly I do—I remember everything!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Listen to me, Pavel Pavlovitch: I have thought it over and have come to very much the same conclusion as you did yourself,” began Velchaninoff gently; “besides—I believe I was a little too irritable towards you last night—too impatient,—I admit it gladly; the fact is—I am not very well sometimes, and your sudden arrival, you know, in the middle of the night——”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “In the middle of the night: you are quite right—it was!” said Pavel Pavlovitch, wagging his head assentingly; “how in the world could I have brought myself to do such a thing? I shouldn’t have come in, though, if you hadn’t opened the door. I should have gone as I came. I called on you about a week ago, and did not find you at home, and I daresay I should never have called again; for I am rather proud—Alexey Ivanovitch—in spite of my present state. Whenever I have met you in the streets I have always said to myself, ‘What if he doesn’t know me and rejects me—nine years is no joke!’ and I did not dare try you for fear of being snubbed. Yesterday, thanks to that sort of thing, you know,” (he pointed to the bottle), “I didn’t know what time it was, and—it’s lucky you are the kind of man you are, Alexey Ivanovitch, or I should despair of preserving your acquaintance, after yesterday! You remember old times, Alexey Ivanovitch!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff listened keenly to all this.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The man seemed to be talking seriously enough, and even with some dignity; and yet he had not believed a single word that Pavel Pavlovitch had uttered from the very first moment that he entered the room.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Tell me, Pavel Pavlovitch,” said Velchaninoff at last, “—I see you are not quite alone here,—whose little girl is that I saw when I came in?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch looked surprised and raised his eyebrow; but he gazed back at Velchaninoff with candour and apparent amiability:

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Whose little girl? Why that’s our Liza!” he said, smiling affably.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “What Liza?” asked Velchaninoff,—and something seemed to cause him to shudder inwardly.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The sensation was dreadfully sudden.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Just now, on entering the room and seeing Liza, he had felt surprised more or less,—but had not been conscious of the slightest feeling of presentiment,—indeed he had had no special thought about the matter, at the moment.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Why—our Liza!—our daughter Liza!” repeated Pavel Pavlovitch, smiling.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Your daughter? Do you mean to say that you and Natalia Vasilievna had children?” asked Velchaninoff timidly, and in a very low tone of voice indeed!

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Of course—but—what a fool I am—how in the world should you know! Providence sent us the gift after you had gone!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch jumped off his chair in apparently pleasurable excitement.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I heard nothing of it!” said Velchaninoff, looking very pale.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “How should you? how should you?” repeated Pavel Pavlovitch with ineffable sweetness.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “We had quite lost hope of any children—as you may remember,—when suddenly Heaven sent us this little one. And, oh! my feelings—Heaven alone knows what I felt! Just a year after you went, I think—no, wait a bit—not a year by a long way!—Let’s see, you left us in October, or November, didn’t you?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I left T—— on the twelfth of September, I remember well.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Hum! September was it? Dear me! Well, then, let’s see—September, October, November, December, January, February, March, April—to the 8th of May—that was Liza’s birthday—eight months all but a bit; and if you could only have seen the dear departed, how rejoiced——”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Show her to me—call her in!” the words seemed to tear themselves from Velchaninoff, whether he liked it or no.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Certainly—this moment!” cried Pavel Pavlovitch, forgetting that he had not finished his previous sentence, or ignoring the fact; and he hastily left the room, and entered the small chamber adjoining.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Three or four minutes passed by, while Velchaninoff heard the rapid interchange of whispers going on, and an occasional rather louder sound of Liza’s voice, apparently entreating her father to leave her alone—so Velchaninoff concluded.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: At last the two came out.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “There you are—she’s dreadfully shy and proud,” said Pavel Pavlovitch; “just like her mother.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Liza entered the room without tears, but with eyes downcast, her father leading her by the hand.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: She was a tall, slight, and very pretty little girl.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: She raised her large blue eyes to the visitor’s face with curiosity; but only glanced surlily at him, and dropped them again.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: There was that in her expression that one always sees in children when they look on some new guest for the first time—retiring to a corner, and looking out at him thence seriously and mistrustingly; only that there was a something in her manner beyond the usual childish mistrust—so, at least thought Velchaninoff.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Her father brought her straight up to the visitor.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “There—this gentleman knew mother very well. He was our friend; you mustn’t be shy,—give him your hand!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The child bowed slightly, and timidly stretched out her hand.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Natalia Vasilievna never would teach her to curtsey; she liked her to bow, English fashion, and give her hand,” explained Pavel Pavlovitch, gazing intently at Velchaninoff.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff knew perfectly well that the other was keenly examining him at this moment, but he made no attempt to conceal his agitation: he sat motionless on his chair and held the child’s hand in his, gazing into her face the while.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: But Liza was apparently much preoccupied, and did not take her eyes off her father’s face; she listened timidly to every word he said.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff recognised her large blue eyes at once; but what specially struck him was the refined pallor of her face, and the colour of her hair; these traits were altogether too significant, in his eyes!

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Her features, on the other hand, and the set of her lips, reminded him keenly of Natalia Vasilievna.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Meanwhile Pavel Pavlovitch was in the middle of some apparently most interesting tale—one of great sentiment seemingly,—but Velchaninoff did not hear a word of it until the last few words struck upon his ear:

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “... So that you can’t imagine what our joy was when Providence sent us this gift, Alexey Ivanovitch! She was everything to me, for I felt that if it should be the will of Heaven to deprive me of my other joy, I should still have Liza left to me; that’s what I felt, sir, I did indeed!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “And Natalia Vasilievna?” asked Velchaninoff.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Oh, Natalia Vasilievna—” began Pavel Pavlovitch, smiling with one side of his mouth; “she never used to like to say much—as you know yourself; but she told me on her deathbed—deathbed! you know, sir—to the very day of her death she used to get so angry and say that they were trying to cure her with a lot of nasty medicines when she had nothing the matter but a simple little feverish attack; and that when Koch arrived (you remember our old doctor Koch?) he would make her all right in a fortnight.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Why, five hours before she died she was talking of fixing that day three weeks for a visit to her Aunt, Liza’s godmother, at her country place!

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff here started from his seat, but still held the child’s hand.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He could not help thinking that there was something reproachful in the girl’s persistent stare in her father’s face.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Is she ill?” he asked hurriedly, and his voice had a strange tone in it.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “No! I don’t think so” said Pavel Pavlovitch; “but, you see our way of living here, and all that: she’s a strange child and very nervous, besides! After her mother’s death she was quite ill and hysterical for a fortnight. Just before you came in she was crying like anything; and do you know what about, sir? Do you hear me, Liza?—You listen!—Simply because I was going out, and wished to leave her behind, and because she said I didn’t love her so well as I used to in her mother’s time. That’s what she pitches into me for! Fancy a child like this getting hold of such an idea!—a child who ought to be playing at dolls, instead of developing ideas of that sort! The thing is, she has no one to play with here.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Then—then—are you two quite alone here?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Quite! a servant comes in once a day, that’s all!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “And when you go out, do you leave her quite alone?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Of course! What else am I to do? Yesterday I locked her in that room, and that’s what all the tears were about this morning. What could I do? the day before yesterday she went down into the yard all by herself, and a boy took a shot at her head with a stone! Not only that, but she must needs go and cling on to everybody she met, and ask where I had gone to! That’s not so very pleasant, you see! But I oughtn’t to complain when I say I am going out for an hour and then stay out till four in the morning, as I did last night! The landlady came and let her out: she had the door broken open! Nice for my feelings, eh! It’s all the result of the eclipse that came over my life; nothing but that, sir!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Papa!” said the child, timidly and anxiously.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Now, then! none of that again! What did I tell you yesterday?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I won’t; I won’t!” cried the child hurriedly, clasping her hands before her entreatingly.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Come! things can’t be allowed to go on in this way!” said Velchaninoff impatiently, and with authority.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “In the first place, you are a man of property; how can you possibly live in a hole like this, and in such disorder?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “This place! Oh, but we shall probably have left this place within a week; and I’ve spent a lot of money here, as it is, though I may be ’a man of property;’ and——”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Very well, that’ll do,” interrupted Velchaninoff with growing impatience, “now, I’ll make you a proposition: you have just said that you intend to stay another week—perhaps two. I have a house here—or rather I know a family where I am as much at home as at my own fireside, and have been so for twenty years. The family I mean is the Pogoryeltseffs—Alexander Pavlovitch Pogoryeltseff is a state councillor (he may be of use to you in your business!) They are now living in the country—they have a beautiful country villa; Claudia Petrovna, the lady of the house, is like a sister—like a mother to me; they have eight children. Let me take Liza down to them without loss of time! they’ll receive her with joy, and they’ll treat her like their own little daughter—they will, indeed!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff was in a great hurry, and much excited, and he did not conceal his feelings.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I’m afraid it’s impossible!” said Pavel Pavlovitch with a grimace, looking straight into his visitor’s eyes, very cunningly, as it seemed to Velchaninoff.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Why! why, impossible?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Oh, why! to let the child go—so suddenly, you know, of course with such a sincere well-wisher as yourself—it’s not that!—but a strange house—and such swells, too!—I don’t know whether they would receive her!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “But I tell you I’m like a son of the house!” cried Velchaninoff, almost angrily.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Claudia Petrovna will be delighted to take her, at one word from me! She’d receive her as though she were my own daughter. Deuce take it, sir, you know you are only humbugging me,—what’s the use of talking about it?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He stamped his foot.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “No—no! I mean to say—don’t it look a little strange? Oughtn’t I to call once or twice first?—such a smart house as you say theirs is—don’t you see——”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I tell you it’s the simplest house in the world; it isn’t ‘smart’ in the least bit,” cried Velchaninoff; “they have a lot of children: it will make another girl of her!—I’ll introduce you there myself, to-morrow, if you like. Of course you’ll have to go and thank them, and all that. You shall go down every day with me, if you please.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Before he had left the town behind him, the carriage was delayed by a block at a cross road, just by a small bridge, over which was passing, at the moment, a long funeral procession.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: There were carriages waiting to move on on both sides of the bridge, and a considerable crowd of foot passengers besides.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The funeral was evidently of some person of considerable importance, for the train of private and hired vehicles was a very long one; and at the window of one of these carriages in the procession Velchaninoff suddenly beheld the face of Pavel Pavlovitch.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff would not have believed his eyes, but that Pavel Pavlovitch nodded his head and smiled to him.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He seemed to be delighted to have recognised Velchaninoff; he even began to kiss his hand out of the window.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff jumped out of his own vehicle, and in spite of policemen, crowd, and everything else, elbowed his way to Pavel Pavlovitch’s carriage window.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He found the latter sitting alone.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “What are you doing?” he cried.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Why didn’t you come to my house? Why are you here?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I’m paying a debt; don’t shout so! I’m repaying a debt,” said Pavel Pavlovitch, giggling and winking.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I’m escorting the mortal remains of my dear friend Stepan Michailovitch Bagantoff!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “What absurdity, you drunken, insane creature,” cried Velchaninoff louder than ever, and beside himself with outraged feeling.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Get out and come with me. Quick! get out instantly!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I can’t. It’s a debt——”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I’ll pull you out, then!” shouted Velchaninoff.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Then I’ll scream, sir, I’ll scream!” giggled Pavel Pavlovitch, as merrily as ever, just as though the whole thing was a joke.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: However, he retreated into the further corner of the carriage, all the same.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Look out, sir, look out! You’ll be knocked down!” cried a policeman.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Sure enough, an outside carriage was making its way on to the bridge from the side, stopping the procession, and causing a commotion.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff was obliged to spring aside, and the press of carriages and people immediately separated him from Pavel Pavlovitch.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He shrugged his shoulders and returned to his own vehicle.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “It’s all the same. I couldn’t take such a fellow with me, anyhow,” he reflected, still all of a tremble with excitement and the rage of disgust.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: When he repeated Maria Sisevna’s story, and his meeting at the funeral, to Claudia Petrovna afterwards, the latter became buried in deep thought.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I am anxious for you,” she said at last.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “You must break off all relations with that man, and as soon as possible.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Oh, he’s nothing but a drunken fool!” cried Velchaninoff passionately; “as if I am to be afraid of him! And how can I break off relations with him? Remember Liza!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Meanwhile Liza was lying ill; fever had set in last night, and an eminent doctor was momentarily expected from town!

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He had been sent for early this morning.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: These news quite upset Velchaninoff.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Claudia Petrovna took him in to see the patient.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I observed her very carefully yesterday,” she said, stopping at the door of Liza’s room before entering it.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “She is a proud and morose child. She is ashamed of being with us, and of having been thrown over by her father. In my opinion that is the whole secret of her illness.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “How ‘thrown over’? Why do you suppose that he has thrown her over?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “The simple fact that he allowed her to come here to a strange house, and with a man who was also a stranger, or nearly so; or, at all events, with whom his relations were such that——”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Oh, but I took her myself, almost by force.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Liza was not surprised to see Velchaninoff alone.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: She only smiled bitterly, and turned her hot face to the wall.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: She made no reply to his passionate promises to bring her father down to-morrow without fail, or to his timid attempts at consolation.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: As soon as Velchaninoff left the sick child’s presence, he burst into tears.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The doctor did not arrive until evening.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: On seeing the patient he frightened everybody by his very first remark, observing that it was a pity he had not been sent for before.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: When informed that the child had only been taken ill last night, he could not believe it at first.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Well, it all depends upon how this night is passed,” he decided at last.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Having made all necessary arrangements, he took his departure, promising to come as early as possible next morning.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff was anxious to stay the night, but Claudia Petrovna begged him to try once more “to bring down that brute of a man.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Try once more!” cried Velchaninoff, passionately; “why, I’ll tie him hand and foot and bring him along myself!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The idea that he would tie Pavel Pavlovitch up and carry him down in his arms overpowered Velchaninoff, and filled him with impatience to execute his frantic desire.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I don’t feel the slightest bit guilty before him any more,” he said to Claudia Petrovna, at parting, “and I withdraw all my servile, abject words of yesterday—all I said to you,” he added, wrathfully.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Liza lay with closed eyes, apparently asleep; she seemed to be better.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: When Velchaninoff bent cautiously over her in order to kiss—if it were but the edge of her bed linen—she suddenly opened her eyes, just as though she had been waiting for him, and whispered, “Take me away!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: It was but a quiet, sad petition—without a trace of yesterday’s irritation; but at the same time there was that in her voice which betrayed that she made the request in the full knowledge that it could not be assented to.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: No sooner did Velchaninoff, in despair, begin to assure her as tenderly as he could that what she desired was impossible, than she silently closed her eyes and said not another word, just as though she neither saw nor heard him.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Arrived in town Velchaninoff told his man to drive him to the Pokrofsky.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: It was ten o’clock at night.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch was not at his lodgings.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff waited for him half an hour, walking up and down the passage in a state of feverish impatience.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Maria Sisevna assured him at last that Pavel Pavlovitch would not come in until the small hours.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Well, then, I’ll return here before daylight,” he said, beside himself with desperation, and he went home to his own rooms.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: What was his amazement, when, on arriving at the gate of his house, he learned from Mavra that “yesterday’s visitor” had been waiting for him ever since before ten o’clock.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “He’s had some tea,” she added, “and sent me for wine again—the same wine as yesterday. He gave me the money to buy it with.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch had made himself very comfortable.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He was sitting in the same chair as he had occupied yesterday, smoking a cigar, and had just poured the fourth and last tumbler of champagne out of the bottle.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The teapot and a half-emptied tumbler of tea stood on the table beside him; his red face beamed with benevolence.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He had taken off his coat, and sat in his shirt sleeves.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Forgive me, dearest of friends,” he cried, catching sight of Velchaninoff, and hastening to put on his coat, “I took it off to make myself thoroughly comfortable.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff approached him menacingly.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “You are not quite tipsy yet, are you? Can you understand what is said to you?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Paul Pavlovitch became a little confused.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “No, not quite. I’ve been thinking of the dear deceased a bit, but I’m not quite drunk yet.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Can you understand what I say?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “My dear sir, I came here on purpose to understand you.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Very well, then I shall begin at once by telling you that you are an ass, sir!” cried Velchaninoff, at the top of his voice.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Why, if you begin that way where will you end, I wonder!” said Pavel Pavlovitch, clearly alarmed more than a little.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff did not listen, but roared again,

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Your daughter is dying—she is very ill! Have you thrown her over altogether, or not?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Oh, surely she isn’t dying yet?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I tell you she’s ill; very, very ill—dangerously ill.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “What, fits? or——”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Don’t talk nonsense. I tell you she is very dangerously ill. You ought to go down, if only for that reason.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “What, to thank your friends, eh? to return thanks for their hospitality? Of course, quite so; I well understand, Alexey Ivanovitch—dearest of friends! He suddenly seized Velchaninoff by both hands, and added with intoxicated sentiment, almost melted to tears, “Alexey Ivanovitch, don’t shout at me—don’t shout at me, please! If you do, I may throw myself into the Neva—I don’t know!—and we have such important things to talk over. There’s lots of time to go to the Pogoryeltseffs another day.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff did his best to restrain his wrath.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “You are drunk, and therefore I don’t understand what you are driving at,” he said sternly.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I’m ready to come to an explanation with you at any moment you like—delighted!—the the sooner the better. But first let me tell you that I am going to take my own measures to secure you. You will sleep here to-night, and to-morrow I shall take you with me to see Liza. I shall not let you go again. I shall bind you, if necessary, and carry you down myself. How do you like this sofa to sleep on?” he added, panting, and indicating a wide, soft divan opposite his own sofa, against the other wall.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Oh—anything will do for me!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Very well, you shall have this sofa. Here, take these things—here are sheets, blankets, pillow” (Velchaninoff pulled all these things out of a cupboard, and tossed them impatiently to Pavel Pavlovitch, who humbly stood and received them); “now then, make your bed,—come, bustle up!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch laden with bed clothes had been standing in the middle of the room with a stupid drunken leer on his face, irresolute; but at Velchaninoff’s second bidding he hurriedly began the task of making his bed, moving the table away from in front of it, and smoothing a sheet over the seat of the divan.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff approached to help him.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He was more or less gratified with his guest’s alarm and submission.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Now, drink up that wine and lie down!” was his next command.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He felt that he must order this man about, he could not help himself.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I suppose you took upon yourself to order this wine, did you?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I did—I did, sir! I sent for the wine, Alexey Ivanovitch, because I knew you would not send out again!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Well, it’s a good thing that you knew that; but I desire that you should know still more. I give you notice that I have taken my own measures for the future, I’m not going to put up with any more of your antics.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Oh, I quite understand, Alexey Ivanovitch, that that sort of thing could only happen once!” said Pavel Pavlovitch, giggling feebly.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: At this reply Velchaninoff, who had been marching up and down the room stopped solemnly before Pavel Pavlovitch.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Pavel Pavlovitch,” he said, “speak plainly! You are a clever fellow—I admit the fact freely,—but I assure you you are going on a false track now. Speak plainly, and act like an honest man, and I give you my word of honour that I will answer all you wish to know.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch grinned his disagreeable grin (which always drove Velchaninoff wild) once more.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Wait!” cried the latter.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “No humbug now, please; I see through you. I repeat that I give you my word of honour to reply candidly to anything you may like to ask, and to give you every sort of satisfaction—reasonable or even unreasonable—that you please. Oh! how I wish I could make you understand me!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Since you are so very kind,” began Pavel Pavlovitch, cautiously bending towards him, “I may tell you that I am very much interested as to what you said yesterday about ‘bird of prey’?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff spat on the ground in utter despair and disgust, and recommenced his walk up and down the room, quicker than ever.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “No, no, Alexey Ivanovitch, don’t spurn my question; you don’t know how interested I am in it. I assure you I came here on purpose to ask you about it. I know I’m speaking indistinctly, but you’ll forgive me that. I’ve read the expression before. Tell me now, was Bagantoff a ‘bird of prey,’ or—the other thing? How is one to distinguish one from the other?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff went on walking up and down, and answered nothing for some minutes.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “The bird of prey, sir,” he began suddenly, stopping in front of Pavel Pavlovitch, and speaking vehemently, “is the man who would poison Bagantoff while drinking champagne with him under the cloak of goodfellowship, as you did with me yesterday, instead of escorting his wretched body to the burial ground as you did—the deuce only knows why, and with what dirty, mean, underhand, petty motives, which only recoil upon yourself and make you viler than you already are. Yes, sir, recoil upon yourself!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Quite so, quite so, I oughtn’t to have gone,” assented Pavel Pavlovitch, “but aren’t you a little——”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “The bird of prey is not a man who goes and learns his grievance off by heart, like a lesson, and whines it about the place, grimacing and posing, and hanging it round other people’s necks, and who spends all his time in such pettifogging. Is it true you wanted to hang yourself? Come, is it true, or not?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I—I don’t know—I may have when I was drunk—I don’t remember. You see, Alexey Ivanovitch, it wouldn’t be quite nice for me to go poisoning people. I’m too high up in the service, and I have money, too, you know—and I may wish to marry again, who knows.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Yes; you’d be sent to Siberia, which would be awkward.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Quite so; though they say the penal servitude is not so bad as it was. But you remind me of an anecdote, Alexey Ivanovitch. I thought of it in the carriage, and meant to tell you afterwards. Well! you may remember Liftsoff at T——. He came while you were there. His younger brother—who is rather a swell, too—was serving at L—— under the governor, and one fine day he happened to quarrel with Colonel Golubenko in the presence of ladies, and of one lady especially. Liftsoff considered himself insulted, but concealed his grievance; and, meanwhile, Golubenko proposed to a certain lady and was accepted. Would you believe it, Liftsoff made great friends with Golubenko, and even volunteered to be best man at his wedding. But when the ceremony was all over, and Liftsoff approached the bridegroom to wish him joy and kiss him, as usual, he took the opportunity of sticking a knife into Golubenko. Fancy! his own best man stuck him! Well, what does the assassin do but run about the room crying. ‘Oh! what have I done? Oh! what have I done?’ says he, and throws himself on everyone’s neck by turns, ladies and all! Ha-ha-ha! He starved to death in Siberia, sir! One is a little sorry for Golubenko; but he recovered, after all.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I don’t understand why you told me that story,” said Velchaninoff, frowning heavily.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Why, because he stuck the other fellow with a knife,” giggled Pavel Pavlovitch, “which proves that he was no type, but an ass of a fellow, who could so forget the ordinary manners of society as to hang around ladies’ necks, and in the presence of the governor, too—and yet he stuck the other fellow. Ha-ha-ha! He did what he intended to do, that’s all, sir!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Go to the devil, will you—you and your miserable humbug—you miserable humbug yourself,” yelled Velchaninoff, wild with rage and fury, and panting so that he could hardly get his words out.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “You think you are going to alarm me, do you, you frightener of children—you mean beast—you low scoundrel you?

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: —scoundrel—scoundrel—scoundrel!

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He had quite forgotten himself in his rage.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch shuddered all over; his drunkenness seemed to vanish in an instant; his lips trembled and shook.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Are you calling me a scoundrel, Alexey Ivanovitch—you—me?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: But Velchaninoff was himself again now.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I’ll apologise if you like,” he said, and relapsed into gloomy silence.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: After a moment he added, “But only on condition that you yourself agree to speak out fully, and at once.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “In your place I should apologise unconditionally, Alexey Ivanovitch.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Very well; so be it then. Velchaninoff was silent again for a while. “I apologise,” he resumed; “but admit yourself, Pavel Pavlovitch, that I need not feel myself in any way bound to you after this. I mean with regard to anything—not only this particular matter.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “All right! Why, what is there to settle between us?” laughed Pavel Pavlovitch, without looking up.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “In that case, so much the better—so much the better. Come, drink up your wine and get into bed, for I shall not let you go now, anyhow.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Oh, my wine—never mind my wine!” muttered Pavel Pavlovitch; but he went to the table all the same, and took up his tumbler of champagne which had long been poured out.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Either he had been drinking copiously before, or there was some other unknown cause at work, but his hand shook so as he drank the wine that a quantity of it was spilled over his waistcoat and the floor.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: However, he drank it all, to the last drop, as though he could not leave the tumbler without emptying it.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He then placed the empty glass on the table, approached his bed, sat down on it, and began to undress.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I think perhaps I had better not sleep here,” he said suddenly, with one boot off, and half undressed.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Well, I don’t think so,” said Velchaninoff, who was walking up and down, without looking at him.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch finished undressing and lay down.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: A quarter of an hour later Velchaninoff also got into bed, and put the candle out.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He soon began to doze uncomfortably.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Some new trouble seemed to have suddenly come over him and worried him, and at the same time he felt a sensation of shame that he could allow himself to be worried by the new trouble.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff was just falling definitely asleep, however, when a rustling sound awoke him.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He immediately glanced at Pavel Pavlovitch’s bed.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The room was quite dark, the blinds being down and curtains drawn; but it seemed to him that Pavel Pavlovitch was not lying in his bed; he seemed to be sitting on the side of it.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “What’s the matter?” cried Velchaninoff.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “A ghost, sir,” said Pavel Pavlovitch, in a low tone, after a few moments of silence.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “What? What sort of a ghost?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Th—there—in that room—just at the door, I seemed to see a ghost!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Whose ghost?” asked Velchaninoff, pausing a minute before putting the question.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Natalia Vasilievna’s!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff jumped out of bed and walked to the door, whence he could see into the room opposite, across the passage.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: There were no curtains in that room, so that it was much lighter than his own.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “There’s nothing there at all. You are drunk; lie down again!” he said, and himself set the example, rolling his blanket around him.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch said nothing, but lay down as he was told.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Did you ever see any ghosts before?” asked Velchaninoff suddenly, ten minutes later.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I think I saw one once,” said Pavel Pavlovitch in the same low voice; after which there was silence once more.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff was not sure whether he had been asleep or not, but an hour or so had passed, when suddenly he was wide awake again.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Was it a rustle that awoke him?

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He could not tell; but one thing was evident—in the midst of the profound darkness of the room something white stood before him; not quite close to him, but about the middle of the room.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He sat up in bed, and stared for a full minute.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Is that you, Pavel Pavlovitch?” he asked.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: His voice sounded very weak.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: There was no reply; but there was not the slightest doubt of the fact that someone was standing there.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Is that you, Pavel Pavlovitch?” cried Velchaninoff again, louder this time; in fact, so loud that if the former had been asleep in bed he must have started up and answered.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: But there was no reply again.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: It seemed to Velchaninoff that the white figure had approached nearer to him.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Then something strange happened; something seemed to “let go” within Velchaninoff’s system, and he commenced to shout at the top of his voice, just as he had done once before this evening, in the wildest and maddest way possible, panting so that he could hardly articulate his words: “If you—drunken ass that you are—dare to think that you could frighten me, I’ll turn my face to the wall, and not look round once the whole night, to show you how little I am afraid of you—a fool like you—if you stand there from now till morning!

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: I despise you!

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: So saying, Velchaninoff twisted round with his face to the wall, rolled his blanket round him, and lay motionless, as though turned to stone.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: A deathlike stillness supervened.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Did the ghost stand where it was, or had it moved?

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He could not tell; but his heart beat, and beat, and beat—At least five minutes went by, and then, not a couple of paces from his bed, there came the feeble voice of Pavel Pavlovitch:

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I got up, Alexey Ivanovitch, to look for a little water. I couldn’t find any, and was just going to look about nearer your bed——”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Then why didn’t you answer when I called?” cried Velchaninoff angrily, after a minute’s pause.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I was frightened; you shouted so, you alarmed me!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

text: “I shall never be there to give you the opportunity,” replied Velchaninoff with a laugh.

text: “I trusted you entirely, sir, solely on account of—all that has passed.”

text: “So that you still consider me the most honourable of men?

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: (Pavel’s eyes seemed to have a special glare in them at this point.)

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Pavel Pavlovitch’s chin suddenly began to tremble.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff was frightened out of his wits.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

text: “Enough, Pavel Pavlovitch!” he said softly, blushing violently and with some show of irritation.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

Yes, sir, that’s the most shameful part of the whole business—the disproportionate nonsense of what you say! You know it’s all humbug; both of us are mean wretches—both of us; and if you like I’ll prove to you at once that not only you don’t love me, but that you loathe and hate me with all your heart, and that you are a liar, whether you know it or not! You took me down to see your bride, not—not a bit in the world to try how she would behave in the society of other men—absurd idea!—You simply saw me, yesterday, and your vile impulse led you to carry me off there in order that you might show me the girl, and say, as it were. There, look at that! She’s to be mine! Try your hand there if you can! It was nothing but your challenge to me! You may not have known it, but this was so, as I say; and you felt the impulse which I have described. Such a challenge could not be made without hatred; consequently you hate me.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I was only anxious to be at peace with you, Alexey Ivanovitch!” said Pavel sadly, his chin and lips working again.

text: “I tell you once more, sir,” he cried, “that you have attached yourself to a sick and irritated man, in order that you may surprise him into saying something unseemly in his madness! We are, I tell you, man, we are men of different worlds. Understand me! between us two there is a grave,” he hissed in his fury, and stopped.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “And how do you know,—sir,” cried Pavel Pavlovitch, his face suddenly becoming all twisted, and deadly white to look at, as he strode up to Velchaninoff, “how do you know what that grave means to me, sir, here!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: (He beat his breast with terrible earnestness, droll though he looked.)

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: But at this moment a loud ring at the bell brought both men to their senses.

text: Someone was ringing so loud that the bell-wire was in danger of snapping.

text: “No more they do for me, sir! I assure you they don’t!” said Pavel Pavlovitch anxiously.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He had become the quiet timid Pavel again in a moment.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff frowned and went to open the door.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Mr. Velchaninoff, if I am not mistaken?” said a strange voice, apparently belonging to some young and very self-satisfied person, at the door.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

text: Velchaninoff felt inclined to send this self-satisfied looking young gentleman flying downstairs again; but he reflected—refrained, stood aside and let him in.

text: A young fellow of some nineteen summers entered the room; he might have been even younger, to judge by his handsome but self-satisfied and very juvenile face.

text: In spite of the pain at his heart Velchaninoff could not help being interested in this impudent youngling.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

text: “I have nowhere to go to, my good sir, I am at home.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “As you like; I confess I should prefer your being present while I have an explanation with this gentleman. Nadejda Fedosievna has given you a flattering enough character, sir, to me.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

You have suddenly come between us as an obstruction; I have come to tell you that you had better clear out of the way at once. Are you prepared to adopt my suggestion?”

text: Pavel Pavlovitch took a step backward in amazement; his face paled visibly, but in a moment a spiteful smile curled his lip.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I said you’d get tired,” remarked the youth.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

Not to speak of myself—there is Nadejda Fedosievna to be considered—the lady to whom you have so impudently attached yourself: that alone is matter sufficient for explanation between us.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: All this the young fellow rattled off carelessly enough, as if the thing were so self-evident that it hardly needed mentioning.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: While talking, he raised his eye-glass once more, and inspected some object for an instant, putting the glass back in his pocket immediately afterwards.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Cheeky young brat!” muttered Velchaninoff.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband

I see your ’business’ is mere childishness and nonsense: to-morrow I shall have the pleasure of an explanation with Mr. Zachlebnikoff, my respected friend. Meanwhile, sir, perhaps you will make it convenient to—depart.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “That’s the sort of man he is,” cried the youth, hotly, turning to Velchaninoff: “he is not content with being as good as kicked out of the place, and having faces made at him, but he must go down again to-morrow to carry tales about us to Mr. Zachlebnikoff. Do you not prove by this, you obstinate man, that you wish to carry off the young lady by force? that you desire to buy her of people who preserve—thanks to the relics of barbarism still triumphant among us—a species of power over her? Surely she showed you sufficiently clearly that she despises you? You have had your wretched tasteless present of to-day—that bracelet thing—returned to you; what more do you want?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Excuse me, no bracelet has been, or can be returned to me,” said Pavel Pavlovitch, with a shudder of anxiety, however.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “How so? hasn’t Mr. Velchaninoff given it to you?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Oh, the deuce take you, sir,” thought Velchaninoff.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Nadejda Fedosievna certainly did give me this case for you, Pavel Pavlovitch,” he said; “I did not wish to take it, but she was anxious that I should: here it is, I’m very sorry.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He took out the case and laid it down on the table before the enraged Pavel Pavlovitch.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “How is it you have not handed it to him before?” asked the young man severely.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I had no time, as you may conclude,” said Velchaninoff with a frown.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “H’m! Strange circumstance!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “What, sir?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Well, you must admit it is strange! However, I am quite prepared to believe that there has been some mistake.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff would have given worlds to get up and drub the impertinent young rascal and drag him out of the house by the ear; but he could not contain himself, and burst out laughing.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: The boy immediately followed suit and laughed too.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: But for Pavel Pavlovitch it was no laughing matter.

text: If Velchaninoff had seen the ferocious look which the former cast at him at the moment when he and Loboff laughed, he would have realized that Pavel Pavlovitch was in the act of passing a fatal limit of forbearance.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: He did not see the look; but it struck him that it was only fair to stand up for Pavel now.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Listen, Mr. Loboff,” he said, in friendly tones, “not to enter into the consideration of other matters, I may point out that Mr. Trusotsky brings with him, in his wooing of Miss Zachlebnikoff, a name and circumstances fully well-known to that esteemed family; in the second place, he brings a fairly respectable position in the world; and thirdly, he brings wealth. Therefore he may well be surprised to find himself confronted by such a rival as yourself—a gentleman of great wealth, doubtless, but at the same time so very young, that he could not possibly look upon you as a serious rival; therefore, again, he is quite right in begging you to bring the conversation to an end.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “What do you mean by ‘so very young’? I was nineteen a month since; by the law I might have been married long ago. That’s a sufficient answer to your argument.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “But what father would consent to allowing his daughter to marry you now—even though you may be a Rothschild to come, or a benefactor to humanity in the future. A man of nineteen years old is not capable of answering for himself and yet you are ready to take on your own responsibility another being—in other words, a being who is as much a child as you are yourself. Why, it is hardly even honourable on your part, is it? I have presumed to address you thus, because you yourself referred the matter to me as a sort of arbiter between yourself and Pavel Pavlovitch.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Yes, by-the-bye, ‘Pavel Pavlovitch,’ I forgot he was called that,” remarked the youth.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I wonder why I thought of him all along as ‘Vassili Petrovitch. Look here, sir (addressing Velchaninoff), you have not surprised me in the least. I knew you were all tarred with one brush. It is strange that you should have been described to me as a man of some originality. However, to business. All that you have said is, of course, utter nonsense; not only is there nothing ‘dishonourable’ about my intentions, as you permitted yourself to suggest, but the fact of the matter is entirely the reverse, as I hope to prove to you by-and-bye. In the first place, we have promised each other marriage, besides which I have given her my word that if she ever repents of her promise she shall have her full liberty to throw me over. I have given her surety to that effect before witnesses.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I bet anything your friend—what’s his name?—Predposiloff invented that idea,” cried Velchaninoff.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “He-he-he!” giggled Pavel Pavlovitch contemptuously.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “What is that person giggling about? You are right, sir, it was Predposiloff’s idea. But I don’t think you and I quite understand one another, do we? and I had such a good report of you. How old are you? Are you fifty yet?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Stick to business, if you please.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Forgive the liberty. I did not mean anything offensive. Well, to proceed. I am no millionaire, and I am no great benefactor to humanity (to reply to your arguments), but I shall manage to keep myself and my wife. Of course I have nothing now; I was brought up, in fact, in their house from my childhood.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “How so?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Oh, because I am a distant relative of this Mr. Zachlebnikoff’s wife. When my people died, he took me in and sent me to school. The old fellow is really quite a kind-hearted man, if you only knew it.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “I do know it!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Yes, he’s an old fogey rather, but a kind-hearted old fellow; but I left him four months ago and began to keep myself. I first joined a railway office at ten roubles a month, and am now in a notary’s place at twenty-five. I made him a formal proposal for her a fortnight since. He first laughed like mad, and afterwards fell into a violent rage, and Nadia was locked up. She bore it heroically. He had been furious with me before for throwing up a post in his department which he procured for me. You see he is a good and kind old fellow at home, but get him in his office and—oh, my word!—he’s a sort of Jupiter Tonans! I told him straight out that I didn’t like his ways; but the great row was—thanks to the second chief at the office; he said I insulted him, but I only told him he was an ignorant beggar. So I threw them all up, and went in for the notary business. Listen to that! What a clap! We shall have a thunder-storm directly! What a good thing I arrived before the rain! I came here on foot, you know, all the way, nearly at a run, too!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “How in the world did you find an opportunity of speaking to Miss Nadia then? especially since you are not allowed to meet.”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Oh, one can always get over the railing; then there’s that red-haired girl, she helps, and Maria Nikitishna—oh, but she’s a snake, that girl! What’s the matter? Are you afraid of the thunder-storm?”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “No, I’m ill—seriously ill!”

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: Velchaninoff had risen from his seat with a fearful sudden pain in his chest, and was trying to walk up and down the room.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
text: “Oh, really! then I’m disturbing you. I shall go at once,” said the youth, jumping up.

title: Uncle's Dream; and The Permanent Husband
